title: Master Shitou
speaker: Sokaku Kathie Fischer
summary: Sokaku Kathie Fischer takes up Shitou Xiqian's Sandokai through Suzuki Roshi's Tassajara lectures, Branching Streams Flow in the Darkness, and the idea of "warm hand to warm hand." Sokaku tells short exchanges among Huineng, Xingse, and Shitou, including Shitou's answer "I don't understand either" when a monk asks about Bodhidharma. Sokaku compares the disappearing "I" to the Heisenberg uncertainty principle and describes Sokaku's own half-asleep sentences as a kaleidoscope of mind. Sokaku reads Suzuki Roshi on sharing another's suffering, notes that Sokaku's husband's toothache is not Sokaku's to feel, and closes with Thich Nhat Hanh's poem "Please Call Me by My True Names."

Madhyamaka has presented a rather thorny logistical case for such teachings as no self, which we know has come down to us as the middle way.
The middle way was the Madhyamaka's work.
The middle way sounds like, but does not mean, a compromise between two extremes, like form and emptiness.
The middle way is not a location.
It means the energetic dynamic of life itself.
Katagiri Roshi, the founder of the Minnesota Zen Center, called it total dynamic work: never static, never fixed, open and always in process.
By the way, how's the sound?
Everybody good back there?
The middle way is expressed in our tradition as not knowing, a statement made by Shitou and subsequent teachers, like in the koan, "not knowing is nearest."
It's expressed as beginner's mind.
In the beginner's mind there are many possibilities.
In the expert's mind there are few.
The Sandokai, translated as harmony of difference and sameness, merging of difference and unity, identity of relative and absolute, and so on, is Shitou's statement of the middle way.
I'm going to give you, first of all, a little bit of background on Shitou, in the form of pithy Zen conversations.
Here we have a conversation between Shitou's teacher, Xingse, and Huineng.
Xingse was one of Huineng's disciples, and Xingse became Shitou's teacher.
So we've got three generations: Huineng, Xingse, and Shitou.
These are hard words.
This sounds all the same, [unclear: "Sherto tafatatatau"].
Don't worry about it.
I'll just keep saying the first, second, and third, so you don't have to keep track.
Xingse asked Huineng.
Xingse is the student of Huineng in this conversation.
So he asks his teacher, "In all that I do, how can I avoid falling into stages of spiritual development?"
In all that I do, how can I avoid falling into stages of spiritual development?
It references a hot controversy of the time, hinted at in the Sandokai as the northern and southern ancestors.
That also touches on the controversy, which has to do with stages of spiritual development.
Are we engaged in stages of spiritual development?
Like, what stage are you on?
I'm going to wear a pin that tells you what stage I'm on.
We don't do that.
Our tradition doesn't teach that way.
However, it doesn't mean that such an approach should never be used, should never be picked up.
You can learn a lot from stages of development.
I'm a recovering schoolteacher, and the school that you all went to, and I taught and I went to, has to do with stages of development.
You can't learn to read without learning the letters.
That's stages of development.
It's our normal way of thinking of learning, and so it's natural that we would bring that normal way to our Zen practice.
But you may have noticed that that normal way is not really what we're doing here.
It's not really what our practice is.
So let's see what he says.
Huineng gets this question from Xingse: "In all that I do, how can I avoid falling into stages of spiritual development?"
And Huineng said, "How do you practice?"
Xingse says, "I don't even practice the Four Noble Truths."
And Huineng says, "What stages have you fallen into?"
Without even studying the Four Noble Truths, what stages could I have fallen into?
And Huineng approved.
We can notice in this conversation that Xingse is not saying he doesn't know and doesn't need to know anything about the Four Noble Truths in order to practice.
He would have studied the Four Noble Truths and other basic Buddhist teachings deeply for many years.
Is this energetic, dynamic moment of life here in this conversation with you?
There are no stages of spiritual development.
There's just you and me.
We have this expression in our lineage, warm hand to warm hand.
In the book of Suzuki Roshi lectures about the Sandokai, his second talk is called Warm Hand to Warm Hand.
Warm hand to warm hand is this not abstract, this absolute immediate, understandable expression of the moments when we meet fully and directly.
Whether a person, a flower, a soup pot in soapy water, there's no separation.
There's no language to describe it.
We're merged, we're submerged in that moment, fully and tenderly.
Yet we are not confused about what is the pot of soapy water and what is me.
This is warm hand to warm hand: two hands meeting as two hands.
And the merging is the warmth.
To go on with another little pithy conversation, I'll tell you first that Shitou was born in 700 and Huineng, I think, died in 713.
Shitou met Huineng when he was a child.
There's a record of a little conversation they had in which Huineng says to him something like, "Well, if you're going to practice with me, you might end up looking as ugly as I am."
That's what Huineng said to Shitou.
And Shitou said, "Fine."
And there was a true meeting.
Sometime later, not very long later, Shitou was at the deathbed of Huineng.
He was present when he died.
He hadn't received his full teaching yet.
And so Xingse, the guy from the previous dialogue, became his teacher.
Now it's after Huineng is gone, and here we have a conversation between Xingse and Shitou.
Again, teacher and student, with Shitou the student.
Xingse says, "Someone says there's news from Lingnan."
Lingnan means south of the mountain, and it would refer to Huineng's temple, something about Huineng's lineage he's teaching.
So again, Xingse says, "Someone says there's news from Lingnan."
And Shitou says, "Someone does say there's news from Lingnan."
Well, this is pure Madhyamaka.
I said the logistical conundrums of Madhyamaka are like this.
Is it true?
Is it not true?
Is it both true and not true?
Is it neither true nor not true?
These are the four statements that are the principles of Madhyamaka.
So he's doing a little dance here.
Again, the question is, "Someone says there's news from Lingnan."
And Shitou says, "Someone does say there's news from Lingnan."
Then Xingse said, "If that's so, then from where did the sutras and shastras come?"
Shastras are all the commentaries and work in the Buddhist canon that are not words attributed directly to Buddha.
The sutras are Buddha's words or words attributed to Buddha.
The shastras are all the other stuff.
So again, Xingse said, "If that's so, then from where did the sutras and shastras come?"
And Shitou said, "They all came."
But we can take a look at this conversation with the relative and absolute in mind.
It seems to come from the relative.
It's about some other place, Lingnan.
It's about some other person who's not present.
And it assumes a passage of time.
There's news that came from this far away place and so on.
It comes from the relative.
So Shitou meets the relative with a statement coming from the absolute.
Someone doesn't say there's news from Lingnan.
He negates the statement.
And then Xingse stands by his statement of the relative by saying, our whole lineage and all the teachings, the relative cannot be disrespected.
It cannot be dismissed.
They all came from the merging of relative and absolute.
Just this energetic, dynamic moment of life as we are here right now.
Shitou is coming back to warm hand to warm hand.
All these sutras and shastras are teachings and records of just this.
You and me, warm hand.
So what is this?
I need a timepiece because I'm still...
Okay, but I have it next to me, because that way I'll...
Thank you, thank you, that's what I need.
What does that come from?
I don't know, but that was a miracle.
A miracle, thank you.
Shitou watch? [unclear: "Shuruto watch"], yeah.
So what is this warm hand?
Warm hand is a living hand, a living person.
Our lineage resides in living beings, conveyed from being to being.
We have a sense that living beings can be trees.
They can be rock, they can be the sky, the moon, the earth's atmosphere, maybe cars, planes, missiles, and bombs.
Find a boundary to this very moment.
There's no boundary.
Here's a couple more pithy dialogues to possibly illustrate or confuse this point.
Now we have Dawu.
I won't tell you about Dawu.
He was very cool.
You should look him up.
Anyway, he said, and this is a dialogue with Shitou, our Shitou, the guy who wrote the Sandokai a long time ago, so we're not sure.
So Dawu says, who is it who has obtained the essential principle of Huineng, who has comprehended the Buddha Dharma?
Dawu says, has the master obtained it?
Shitou says, I haven't attained it.
Dawu says, why haven't you attained it?
And Shitou says, because I can't comprehend the Buddha Dharma.
A monk asks Shitou, why did the first ancestor come from the West?
He's talking about Bodhidharma.
Shitou says, ask the temple pillar.
The monk says, I don't understand.
Shitou says, I don't understand either.
So these dialogues resonate with the previous conversation in which Shitou's teacher, Xingsi, says, I don't even practice the Four Noble Truths.
Comprehending Buddha Dharma cannot be attained by a sense of I.
A separate I who acquires knowledge and attainment disappears in the comprehension of Buddha Dharma.
It's like the Heisenberg Uncertainty Principle: the position and the velocity of a particle cannot be measured at the same time.
You can look at its position, but you can't at the same time look at its velocity.
You can look at its velocity, but you can't at the same time look at its position.
And there's nothing wrong with position, and there's nothing wrong with velocity.
It's not like one's better than the other.
It's just that you look at one or the other.
And the sense of these dialogues is, it's the same with I.
I steps aside when comprehension of Buddha Dharma is present, and comprehension of Buddha Dharma steps aside when I is present, when it's time to go make lunch.
You want I.
I knows where the soup pot is.
So there's this sense of warm hand to warm hand, the fluidity of the human mind.
I is present.
We study in Buddhism the sense of I as a fabrication of mind.
It's necessary, but it's a fabrication.
And we should not diminish or disrespect a sense of order, a sense of past and future, predictability.
It is really important in our lives.
We need to show up on time for appointments.
We need to put them in our calendar for next week so that we'll show up.
That's our life.
I want the pot to be where it belongs.
I don't want to have to go searching for the pot.
We have this sense of an I and a sense of past, present, and future.
The teaching of the Sandokai is about the merging, the identity of relative and absolute, or the merging of relative and absolute.
And it's not a steady state.
There are no steady states.
Through our work, we can open wide to the moments of, oh, it's not here.
It's time to be open.
We can do that sometimes.
We'll let go of annoyance and move on to the next adventure.
And in washing the pot, I can disappear into the beauty of the soapy water.
The sense of I as a fabrication was illustrated to me recently as I was falling asleep.
The sentences of my narrative were falling apart into fragments.
And so I thought, "She walks up in the apple tree, getting done.
Do I love you?
Mine or mine?
A stone's throw.
Swim along."
But mind is a storyteller.
I have evolved a mind which is an incessant storyteller, like a kaleidoscope, making ever-changing patterns from random disparate elements.
Another night I actually got up and wrote down my best recollection of one of these kaleidoscopic constructions.
Here's what I wrote: "When I was six, he gave me miso with tempeh.
And I gave it to my mother, who rewarded me with a lipstick and said, you are perfect just the way you are, but still you could use a little improvement."
So this sentence sounds like it makes sense, but it doesn't.
It makes no sense.
It references events of many decades.
And our language is an expression of mind.
Our language is like a kaleidoscope.
It can integrate disparate elements so that they appear to make sense.
But I really do love the thought of my mother speaking to me: have a lipstick.
Norman wrote a book of poetry years ago called *On Whether or Not to Believe in Your Mind*.
We act on our kaleidoscopic thoughts, products of mind, with deep belief in their truth.
And it makes the world so dangerous.
But after all, that's all we've got.
And it's miraculous that it works as well as it does to get things done.
The dishes washed should not be diminished.
Our practice is to see mind as it is, to bring mind to our practice and the work of mind and body to our practice.
We're not here to whip mind and body into the shape of practice.
Mind and body are our offering.
Practice and enlightenment should not be the bullies.
When we make practice and enlightenment the bullies, we might not notice the ordinary moments, the humdrum moments, the yucky moments, which are, in and of themselves, extraordinary.
I'd like to read a passage from Suzuki Roshi's talk entitled "Warm Hand to Warm Hand."
He's speaking about our bodhisattva work in relation to others.
He says:
*If someone is very good, we can share the joy of practice with them by giving them a good cushion, a good zendo, something like that.
But a zendo doesn't mean anything to someone who is suffering.
Whatever you give may not be accepted.
And they say, I don't need it.
I'm suffering too much.
I don't know why.
Right now to get out of the suffering is the most important.
When you hear this, you should be like Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva.
You should become like the one who is suffering.
And you should suffer as that person suffers.
Because of your innate love, your instinctive love, you share the suffering.
That is love in its true sense.*
So this is a scary practice.
Not being bullied by our commitment to helping or to our idea of what help and goodness is supposed to be.
Just responding, warm hand to warm hand.
We see a number of paired words and images: west to east, sharp or dull, northern or southern ancestors, light and dark.
Spiritual source and branching streams interact and do not.
The nature of relationships.
Not one, not two.
Shimmering dynamism of relationship.
We can't really say much about objects without implying their relations with other objects, relation to space, energy and so on.
And we can't favor one over another because they are interdependent.
Light and dark oppose one another like front and back foot in walking.
As Tim said the other day, the opposition of weight, balance and momentum is what walking is.
Shohaku Okumura likens this analogy to the five fingers of your hand.
Each finger is separate and yet not separate.
Each finger is a part of the hand and each finger has its own capacity.
The little finger cannot do what the index finger can do.
Yet it would be absurd to try to figure out which is more important, higher ranking, more worthy of our practice.
This makes no sense.
These pairings refer to value judgments inherent in teachings in other schools during the Tang dynasty.
Most of those other schools have faded into history.
But today we still have our deep value judgments about things, about people, about groups of people and so on.
And these make our world deep.
For now I'd like to leave us with the one point about the Sandokai: that things exist in relationship, interrelationship and interdependent.

Shohaku Okumura speaks of his wife and I'll speak of my husband, making the point that even though I know and love my husband, having been married for 47 years, still if he has a toothache I cannot feel the pain.
He and I will each die alone, even if one or the other of us is present.
This bears responsibility for our actions.
Those of us who have taken bodhisattva vows are responsible for understanding to the best of our ability and for carrying the teachings forth according to our particular circumstances.

Yet we walk forward in this together, sharing, merging, enriching each other's lives, and we bear responsibility for the world we wake up in: to rejoice with the joyous, grieve with the grieving and to see what is needed that I can find.
Again our hearts are breaking with the violence and suffering.
And in that spirit I would like to end with this wonderful, time-honored poem.
*Please call me by my true names.
Don't say that I will depart tomorrow.
Even today I am still arriving.
Look deeply.
Every second I am arriving.
To be a bud on a spring branch.
To be a tiny bird with still fragile wings, learning to sing in my new nest.
To be a caterpillar in the heart of a flower.
To be a jewel hiding itself in a stone.
I still arrive in order to laugh and to cry, to fear and to hope.
The rhythm of my heart is the birth and death of all that is alive.*
*I am the mayfly metamorphosing on the surface of the river.
And I am the bird that swoops down to swallow the mayfly.
I am the frog swimming happily in the clear water of a pond.
And I am the grass snake that silently feeds itself on the frog.
I am the child in Uganda, all skin and bones, my legs as thin as bamboo sticks.
I am the arms merchant selling deadly weapons to Uganda.
I am the 12-year-old girl refugee on a small boat who throws herself into the ocean after being raped by a sea pirate.
And I am the pirate, my heart not yet capable of seeing and loving.*
*I am a member of the politburo with plenty of power in my hands.
And I am the man who has to pay his debt of blood to my people, dying slowly in a forced labor camp.
My joy is like spring, so warm it makes flowers bloom all over the earth.
My pain is like a river of tears, so vast it fills the four oceans.*
*Please call me by my true names so I can hear all my cries and my laughter at once.
So I can see that my joy and pain are one.
Please call me by my true names so I can wake up and so the door of my heart can be left open.
The door of compassion.*
